question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens when the opponent shouts 'fault!' during your shot. itto-5.9.1.4 covers exactly this: a player calling 'fault' to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke is a deliberate distraction under Law 13.4.5. laws-13.4.5 confirms that in play, a player who deliberately distracts an opponent by shouting commits a fault under Law 13.4. laws-7.3 gives the consequence: a side wins the rally if the opposing side commits a fault, and the side winning a rally adds a point. So the opponent's shout is a fault by the opponent, you win the rally and score a point. itto-5.9.1.3 (shouting to a partner) does not apply because the shout was directed at the opponent.
answer.answer: Your opponent's shout of 'fault!' while you were playing your shot is a fault by your opponent. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), "A player calling ‘fault’, etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)", and under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Law 13.4.5, "if, in play, a player: deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures" commits a fault under Law 13.4. The consequence follows from Law 7.3 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2): "A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a ‘fault’", and "The side winning a rally shall add a point to its score." So you win the rally and score a point against your opponent.

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) what happens when a let occurs (the replay) — answered by laws-14.3, with laws-14.1 covering who calls it; (2) every situation that counts as a let — answered by laws-14.2 and its sub-clauses laws-14.2.1 through laws-14.2.7, where laws-14.2.3 ends with a colon and is expanded by laws-14.2.3.1 and laws-14.2.3.2 (read to confirm). itto-5.9.1.2 adds a qualification about a shuttle from an adjacent court. Searches confirmed no further 14.2.x clauses exist beyond 14.2.7. All parts have sources, so refused is false.
answer.answer: A 'let' is called by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire, to halt play (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Law 14.1). When a 'let' occurs, the rally is replayed: play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again (Law 14.3). Under Law 14.2 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), it shall be a 'let' if: (1) the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4) (14.2.1); (2) during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted (14.2.2); (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is caught on the net and remains suspended on its top (14.2.3.1), or after passing over the net is caught in the net (14.2.3.2); (4) during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle (14.2.4); (5) in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach (14.2.5); (6) a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision (14.2.6); or (7) any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred (14.2.7). Note from the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.9.1.2: a shuttle coming onto the court from an adjacent court shall not automatically be considered a 'let', and a 'let' shall not be called in such circumstances if, in the opinion of the Umpire, the shuttle has not obstructed or distracted the players.

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play may stop for a bleeding injury, and (2) who may come on court to help. Part 1 is answered by itto-5.14.2 (delay until bleeding stops, wound dressed, or Referee advises otherwise), itto-3.6.1.4 (Referee resolves well within a few minutes, with possible disqualification warning), itto-5.14.1 (no treatment causing undue delay; Umpire times the delay), and itto-3.6.1.2 (quick relief such as a bandage allowed; no time-consuming treatment except in regular intervals). Part 2 is answered by itto-3.6.1.1 (Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court immediately when called), itto-5.14.1 (Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required), and itto-3.6.1.3 (maximum two persons on court to assist/advise/translate, with the same consideration for the opposing side). Both parts have sources, so refused is false.
answer.answer: For your partner's bleeding hand, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.14.2). The Referee shall resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned, and may point to potential disqualification if it is suspected that the player is exploiting the injury situation to regain wind or repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon play (Clause 3.6.1.4). No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court, and the Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury (Clause 5.14.1). The Tournament Doctor may apply a quick relief, such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals, and then only if the Tournament Doctor estimates that the treatment can be completed (or nearly so) before the interval ends (Clause 3.6.1.2). As for who may come on court: when called by the Umpire in case of injury, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court (Clause 3.6.1.1), and the Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court (Clause 5.14.1). The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation, and in fairness shall allow the opposing side the same consideration (Clause 3.6.1.3).

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: what happens to the match when water makes the court unplayable mid-game, and what happens to the score. Sources cover both: Laws 16.3.1/16.3.3 cover suspension and score standing; ITTO 5.11.2/5.11.3/5.11.4/5.11.5 cover the umpire's suspension procedure and resumption. No part is missing.
answer.answer: Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, water dripping onto the court is a circumstance not within the players’ control, so “the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary.” Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, if during a match “a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.” When play is suspended, “the Umpire shall call: ‘Play is suspended’ and note ‘S’ on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.” For the score, under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, “If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point,” so the suspension awards no point to you or to your opponent. When play resumes, under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, “the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call ‘Are you ready?’ followed by the score and ‘Play’.”

citations.quote: When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary.

If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.
When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.
If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.

When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what the umpire can do when the opponent repeatedly flicks sweat onto the court. itto-5.9.1.6 directly covers a player throwing sweat or contaminating the court: the umpire shall remind the player the conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied if necessary. laws-16.7.1 and its children (16.7.1.1–16.7.1.3) give the escalation steps for a breach of Law 16.6: warning, faulting if previously warned, or faulting for a flagrant offence. laws-16.7.2 adds that on faulting a side the umpire reports the offending side immediately to the Referee, who may disqualify that side. itto-3.6.2 confirms the Referee is called for flagrant misbehaviour resulting in a red card. All parts of the question are covered; nothing is missing.
answer.answer: The umpire shall remind your opponent that throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied if necessary (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.9.1.6). Under Law 16.7.1 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), the umpire administers a breach of Law 16.6 by issuing a warning to the offending side, or faulting the offending side if previously warned, or faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach. Because your opponent keeps doing it, once a warning has been issued the umpire faults your opponent's side. On faulting a side, the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match (Law 16.7.2). The Referee is also called on court in case of flagrant misbehaviour resulting in a red card (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 3.6.2).

citations.quote: A player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied, if necessary; and
The umpire shall administer any breach of Law 16.2, 16.4.1, 16.5.2 or 16.6 by:
issuing a warning to the offending side; or
faulting the offending side, if previously warned; or
faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach.
On faulting a side (Law 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3), the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question has three parts: what the line judge does when unsighted, who decides the call then, and what happens to the rally if no decision can be made. itto-8.5 and itto-8.8 cover the unsighted signal; itto-2.5 and itto-5.8.3 (with 5.8.3.1–5.8.3.3) cover the Umpire making the decision when the Line Judge is unsighted; laws-14.2.6, itto-2.5, itto-5.8.9 and laws-14.3 cover the let and its effect on the rally. All parts are sourced.
answer.answer: The Line Judge must signal that they were unsighted: "If unsighted, inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes" (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 8.5), and "UNSIGHTED" is one of "The approved hand signals" (Clause 8.8). The Umpire then makes the decision: "When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision" (Clause 2.5), and "Where there is no Line Judge or if a Line Judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately call" (Clause 5.8.3) — "'Out' when the shuttle lands outside the line" (5.8.3.1), the score or "Service over" and then the score when it lands "in" (5.8.3.2), or "'Let' followed by the score when the Umpire is unsighted" (5.8.3.3). If no decision can be made, the rally becomes a let: "It shall be a 'let', if: a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision" (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 14.2.6), and "When no decision can be made, a 'let' shall be called ... unless IRS is in use, in which case it will be used to decide on the line call" (ITTO Clause 2.5); if the IRS indicates "NO DECISION", "it shall be a 'Let' if the original call is 'Unsighted'" (ITTO Clause 5.8.9). When a let occurs, "play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again" (Laws Clause 14.3), so the rally is replayed from the same service.

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand court-side during a match. itto-5.12.2 directly answers this: coaches must be seated in designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during permitted intervals (Law 16.2). The permitted intervals are defined in laws-16.2.1 (60 seconds at 11 points each game) and laws-16.2.2 (120 seconds between games). itto-5.12.3 concerns moving the chair, not standing, so it is not needed. All parts of the question are covered.
answer.answer: No. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, your coach "must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2)" [itto-5.12.2]. The only times your coach may stand court-side are the permitted intervals under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26: "not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points, except Handicap matches" [laws-16.2.1], and "not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game, and between the second and third game" [laws-16.2.2].

question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts. (1) Whether a pre-'Play' yellow card costs a point now: itto-5.17.10 directly covers misconduct before 'Play' on the Field of Play and states any card given has no effect on the score of the match but is taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2). (2) Whether the card goes on the record after the tournament: itto-3.7.3 states the Referee sends to BWF (or CC) immediately after the tournament a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions; itto-5.17.2 has the Umpire record and report the misconduct to the Referee. Both parts are answered; no part is missing.
answer.answer: No, the yellow card does not cost your opponent a point now: for misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before "Play" has been called, "Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match but a card(s) shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match" (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.17.10). The card does carry consequences after the match: the Umpire must "Record and report to the Referee any incident of misconduct and the action taken" (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.17.2), and "The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions" (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 3.7.3). So the yellow card against your opponent is reported after the tournament and may trigger further sanctions, but it does not affect the score of the match in which it was given.
